newsitem.title: UK: Europe crude outlook-weak margins to smother rally.
newsitem.headline: Europe crude outlook-weak margins to smother rally.

text.p: Slim refining margins are expected to take some of the muscle out of the North Sea crude market this week, but most traders were reluctant to predict a wholesale slump in prices having been taken by surprise by last week's startling rally in physical differentials.
"I very much doubt if it's going to go any higher, but then I would never have expected it to get as strong as this," said one North Sea crude trader.
A benchmark Dated Brent cargo fetched a premium of 48 cents to March Brent paper on Friday, a climb of 35 cents on a March-related deal struck at the beginning of the week.
All three Brent cargoes nominated from the paper chains on Friday were kept, with two quickly sold on, underscoring the market's bullish tone.
Buyers seeking to cover prompt shorts had little choice but to bid the market up late last week with the early February market all but sold out, market-watchers said.
"There's nothing on the Brent side left for the first decade, while Forties and Oseberg are committed well into the second decade," said a trader.
Nevertheless, strong crude prices have translated into even weaker margins for refiners.
Profit margins at a typical northwest European refinery were running at just 15 cents a barrel on Friday, having shed some 25 cents in a week.
"(The market) has reached its peak...margins are lousy. I find it impossible to believe it can go anywhere but down," said a more bearish trader at a European major.
"Most of the demand has been met and now Ekofisk is back things are starting to loosen up," he added.
Production at the 350,000 barrel per day Ekofisk field was restarted on Tuesday after a week's shutdown due to a gas leak in an oil pipeline.
But although a rush of delayed Ekofisk loadings are expected in the last days of the month, the February programme, released on Friday, scheduled a reduction of 30,000 bpd of liftings from January.
In the Mediterranean, Russian Urals was expected to climb this week above recent traded levels in the (Dated Brent) -70s.
"It's certainly in the 60s now. I don't think it's going to go back into the 70s in the short term."
While sour margins were also slackening, Med refiners said that Urals would remain the most profitable of the sour grades even at slightly firmer differentials.

The outlook for West African grades was divided, with gasoline-yielding crudes such as Brass River expected to build on recent gains, which saw a cargo trade as high as Dated Brent +72 cents late last week.
But distillate-rich grades such as Forcados could start to could come under pressure, dealers said.
"Forcados is a heating oil grade, and if you're selling into the States it takes 35 days...by then it's starting to come out of winter," said one trader active in the West African market.
The possibility of South Korean refinery run cuts could also quell demand, traders said.
